The Unity CLI 1.0 is here!
==========================

Nov 17, 2026|5 Min

Christopher Addison - Unity Technologies

Senior Software Developer

AIAI features

AIAI features

![Unity CLI 1.0](https://mip.web.unity.com/img/E_-DwkiCrvrmky4PUv2wJvY-hmyudGmHc5kVTDd44oY/w:1609/h:965/r:0,7,1609,965/q:75/f:avif/aHR0cHM6Ly9jZG4uc2FuaXR5LmlvL2ltYWdlcy9mdXZiampscC9wcm9kdWN0aW9uLzMzMDhmOWY4Mzk3ZDNmOWVhZGYzYTkxY2NkM2RlMzc1NGZkODI0MDAtMTYwOXg5NzgucG5n.avif)

On July 15, 2026, we brought Unity to the [terminal](https://discussions.unity.com/t/announcing-the-unity-cli-a-new-way-to-connect-your-tools-and-agents/1731104). Today at Unite Tokyo, the Unity CLI and the [Pipeline package](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/unity-pipeline/unity-pipeline-package) (`com.unity.pipeline`) are out of beta. Version 1.0 is ready for your projects, your build machines and your agents.

### How we got here

We started with a beta: one binary that installs and manages Unity Editors, modules and projects from the terminal, which we introduced in [Meet the Unity CLI](/blog/meet-the-unity-cli). Alongside it, the Pipeline package lets the CLI drive a running Editor on your machine, so a script or an agent could open a project, run a command and check the result.

Next, the Unity Hub started installing the CLI for you, so if you're on the latest Hub, you already have it. Then came official Unity plugins for [Claude Code](/blog/unity-plugin-for-claude-code), [Codex](/blog/unity-plugin-codex), [Grok Build](/blog/unity-plugin-grok) and [Google Antigravity](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/ai/unity-plugin/antigravity), which give those agents skills written by Unity's own teams. The same skills are public in the [Unity skills repository on GitHub](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/skills), so any agent can use them.

Along the way, we shipped more than 17 beta releases, shaped by what you told us.

### Inside the Unity CLI

Since July 20, more than **350,000** logged-in users have run more than **600 million commands** with the Unity CLI. About 98% of those runs come from coding agents and other automation.

We looked closer at that usage in [what we've learned about how developers use the Unity CLI](/blog/unity-cli-usage-data-ai-coding-agents): people set Unity up, then their agent does the work inside a live Editor.

### What you told us

Many of the changes in 1.0 started as a bug report, a Discussions thread or a message from a studio using the CLI every day.

_"I am not exaggerating when I say the CLI has completely changed how I work with Unity. It is incredible."_ Dorado Digital

_"The CLI is crazy good in the most simplistic way. I'm still very much holding the reins for the moment, but it's really positive."_ Andy, Kwalee

Studios also sent us detailed reports: commands that said they succeeded when they hadn't, dialogs that blocked a remote session, scripts that broke when output changed shape. That feedback set the priorities for the releases that followed. You can read every change in the [Unity CLI release notes](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/release-notes) or run `unity changelog`.

### What changed since launch

*   **One command to set up your agent.** `unity setup` installs the official plugin for Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build or Google Antigravity. `unity skill install --all` gives Unity's skills to every agent on the machine, including VS Code, GitHub Copilot, Qwen Code and OpenCode, and `unity skill sync` keeps them current. The install script now adds Unity's skills to every agent it finds.
*   **No more sessions stuck on a hidden dialog.** The CLI can now see the dialog an Editor is waiting on and answer it, so a script or an agent doesn't hang on a popup nobody can see.
*   **Builds through the Editor you already have open.** `unity build --target` builds in the Editor that has the project open, and `unity pipeline cloud-build` sets up cloud build targets from the terminal.
*   **Version control that reads like a person would.** `unity vcs` names the asset behind each change in a scene or prefab, and can summarize a pull request without switching branches.
*   **New projects that are ready from the start.** `unity projects create` adds the Pipeline package to every new project, and can install the Editor the project needs. `unity open --until-ready` waits until the Editor can take commands.
*   **Output scripts can rely on.** Every listing and stream now has the same JSON shape. Short flags mean the same thing in every command, `--project-path` works everywhere, and the CLI never prompts in CI. Clear exit codes tell a script when the Editor is busy, when a dialog is blocking it or when the network is down. You can pin a CLI version range per project.
*   **A health check for your project.** `unity projects audit` runs Project Auditor and writes a report, with a focus such as upgrades, optimization or URP.
*   **Easier to install and keep current.** The CLI is a native binary on macOS, Linux and Windows, available through Homebrew, winget and APT. `unity self-update` keeps your last three versions, so you can roll back. You can also keep the docs offline with `unity docs cache add`.
*   **Hardened for teams.** Security fixes across installs, skills and project linking, so a cloned repository can't run its own programs in place of the real ones.

**1.0 is also a commitment:** commands, flags and output stay compatible across 1.x releases. When something has to change, you’ll get a deprecation warning and time to update before anything is removed.

### Use it with your agents

The CLI is how an agent actually works with Unity: it opens the project, runs commands in the Editor, enters Play mode and reads the result. With the official Unity plugin, the agent also gets Unity's own skills for tasks like building UI, setting up lighting or [adding in-app purchases](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/ai/unity-plugin/about-unity-plugin). See the [Unity plugin documentation](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/ai/unity-plugin/about-unity-plugin) for the full list.

Agents without an official plugin still work in Unity through the CLI. So do scripts, test runners and CI jobs with no AI involved at all. To see it in action, watch the [Automate with Unity CLI livestream](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Iruqwhn6w-o).

Agents and automation are also getting a supported place to run. The Build Server license now covers agents and automation, not only builds: one license per instance lets you run agents on a headless Editor or in a container, on any computer.

Coming soon: the Linux containerized Editor, a supported headless Unity Editor in a Linux container, built for CI, build machines and agents.

### What’s next?

We’ll keep shipping updates the way we did during the beta. Next, we’re bringing more of Unity to the terminal: commands for AI Generators, Live Games and Build Automation, and accounts built for agents.

### Get started

If you're on the latest Unity Hub, you already have the CLI. Open a terminal and start with the [Unity CLI documentation](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/unity-cli). New to the terminal? Try [A beginner's guide to Unity CLI and the Pipeline package](/resources/a-beginners-guide-to-unity-cli-and-the-pipeline-package), or the [Unity CLI introduction video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DgNrgZeJOxQ).

And keep telling us what you build: your feedback shaped 1.0, and it will shape what comes next.

Meet the Unity CLI: manage Unity from your terminal
===================================================

Jul 20, 2026

![](https://mip.web.unity.com/img/p9dPjXgqWVKt-UEuK3Btpk4ru1V8ttF980lF2ALkuUU/w:450/h:450/q:75/f:avif/aHR0cHM6Ly9jZG4uc2FuaXR5LmlvL2ltYWdlcy9mdXZiampscC9wcm9kdWN0aW9uLzcwZTM4ZTA4MzhhMzcyODA3ZGUwYjMxMDE2OWJlMDc1MTE0MmMzYWEtNDUweDQ1MC5wbmc.avif?w=96)2 authorsMore details

TL;DR
-----

*   **Available now**: the **Unity CLI** is a standalone _unity_ binary for managing and interacting with editors, modules, projects, and auth from the terminal. No UI needed; install via command line.
*   Built for automation: structured JSON/TSV output, clear exit codes, non-interactive installs, and service-account auth for CI.
*   **Also available today**: the experimental _com.unity.pipeline_ package lets the CLI drive a running Editor, or a dev Player build, over a local API. You can expose your own commands with a _\[CliCommand\]_ attribute.
*   _unity command eval_ runs C# code live inside a running Editor or Player and returns the result, with no project-level recompile or domain reload required.
*   Together, they allow AI agents to operate Unity: observe a live project, act on it, and verify the result.
*   If you’d prefer to watch a video overview of the Unity CLI, [you can do so here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DgNrgZeJOxQ).

More and more of development happens in the terminal: in scripts, in CI, and increasingly in the hands of AI agents. Today Unity meets you there. The **Unity CLI** brings Unity to the terminal at every level: install and manage editors with one binary, drive a running Editor from a script, and even execute live C# inside your project with no recompile. It's one single, fast unity command, and each layer goes further than the last: the CLI manages Unity, the Pipeline package drives it, and eval reaches inside it. Both the CLI and the Pipeline package are available today.

Before we dig into things, let’s take a look at what is possible when these features come together:

_In this 25-second clip, a developer hands an AI agent a plain-English bug report: "the player sometimes falls through the floor." The agent uses unity command eval <code> to inspect the live scene, finds a collider disabled at runtime, re-enables it, and re-enters Play mode to confirm the fix, observing the running game, acting on it, and verifying the result itself, with no copy-pasting of console output._

What is the Unity CLI
---------------------

The CLI ships as a single self-contained binary. There are no dependencies to install, and installation adds itself to your PATH: simply run it as _unity_, and update it in place with _unity upgrade_. Beyond editors and projects, it also handles modules and authentication, so a fresh machine needs nothing else.

Because it's a native binary, it starts quickly, whereas the old Unity Hub headless path (_\-- --headless_) took noticeably longer. This gap adds up across the dozens of calls a script or agent makes per job.

Get started
-----------

Install it with your platform’s package manager:

    # macOS or Linux
    curl -fsSL https://public-cdn.cloud.unity3d.com/hub/prod/cli/install.sh | UNITY_CLI_CHANNEL=beta bash
    
    # Windows
    $env:UNITY_CLI_CHANNEL='beta'; irm https://public-cdn.cloud.unity3d.com/hub/prod/cli/install.ps1 | iex

_(Note: Support for standard package managers like brew, winget and apt is coming soon. Refer to the [CLI documentation](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/use-unity-cli) for the latest.)_

Explore what's available:

    unity --help

Installing an editor with the modules you need is a one-liner:

    unity install 6000.2.10f1 -m android ios webgl

From there, commands read the way you'd expect: _unity editors_ to see what's installed, _unity open_ to launch a project with the right editor resolved, and _unity auth login_ to sign in. Not sure which module IDs a version has? _unity modules list 6000.2.10f1_ has you covered.

Built for automation
--------------------

The CLI was built to live inside automation, not just an interactive shell. Every command can emit structured output you can pipe straight into your tooling:

    unity editors --format json
    unity editors --format tsv

Errors go to _stderr_, results to _stdout_, and exit codes follow a simple contract (_0_ success, _1_ error, _130_ cancelled), so failures are easy to catch in a pipeline.

For unattended installs, skip every prompt:

    unity install 6000.2.10f1 -m android ios --accept-eula --yes

On a headless build agent, it authenticates with a service account via environment variables. No browser, no manual step. And _unity doctor_ diagnoses environment, credential, and configuration problems.

Talking to the Editor
---------------------

Managing installs is only half the story. The Unity CLI can also drive a _running_ Editor.

Once added to a project, _com.unity.pipeline_ lets a running Editor receive commands from the CLI entirely on your machine. It works with Unity 6.0 LTS and newer, and turns the Editor into a programmable automation target for scripts, CI jobs, and agentic tools.

Adding it to a project is a single command:

    unity pipeline install

You can check which of your projects have it installed with _unity pipeline list_. With the package in place, you can execute registered commands against a connected Editor (or even a Player runtime) directly from the terminal:

    # List the commands a connected Editor exposes
    unity command
    
    # Run one of them
    unity command <command-name>

Those commands aren't a fixed set. Any static method in your project becomes one by adding a _\[CliCommand\]_ attribute, with _\[CliArg\]_ on its parameters:

    using Unity.Pipeline.Commands;
    using UnityEngine;
    
    public static class MyPipelineCommands
    {
        [CliCommand("greet", "Log a greeting and return its length")]
        public static int Greet(
            [CliArg("name", "Who to greet", Required = true)] string name)
        {
            Debug.Log($"Hello, {name}!");
            return name.Length;
        }
    }

The package discovers it automatically, with no registration step. _unity command greet --name World_ runs it against the connected Editor and hands back the result.

The Pipeline package is available today. It is currently **experimental**, so expect it to evolve. It lets you automate what used to require a human in the Editor: triggering imports, running tests, custom tooling.

It doesn't stop at the Editor. Drop its runtime component into a development build and your _running game_ exposes the same kind of API. Point the CLI at it with _unity command --runtime <player exec name>_ to pull live logs, query runtime status, or hot-reload code in a build that's already playing. It's localhost-only and off by default (for dev and QA builds, never production), but it turns a running Player into something a script, test rig, or AI agent can drive in a live runtime instance.

Unity CLI<->running Editor via com.unity.pipeline

### Execute C# scripts with _eval_

Registered commands cover the operations you've anticipated. _unity command eval_ covers the ones you haven't. It evaluates an arbitrary C# expression _inside_ a running Editor and hands you back the result: a live Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL) into your project, from the terminal.

    unity command eval "return Application.version;"
    unity command eval "return UnityEditor.EditorApplication.isPlaying;"
    unity command eval "var s = Application.dataPath; return s.Length;" --json
    unity command eval_file "path/to/script.cs"

It's compiled with Roslyn and run on the Editor's main thread, so it reaches any engine or editor API your project can, and the same _\--runtime_ flag aims it at a live Player. Because that power cuts both ways, eval is gated behind a security token. No predefined command, no plugin, no recompile: if you can express a question in C#, you can ask a running Unity instance.

The advantage is speed. The usual change-and-check cycle (edit, recompile, relaunch) costs seconds at best; _eval_ answers in milliseconds against an instance that's already up. Across the many calls a script or an agent makes in a session, that difference adds up, and it’s exactly what gives an AI agent a tight feedback loop instead of a slow one.

![Iterate in a fraction of the time](https://mip.web.unity.com/img/OC8HHcsOxBqrF3l6LgXd1AVyhIm7m0EEbuNzy1S5AQo/w:2400/h:1260/q:75/f:avif/aHR0cHM6Ly9jZG4uc2FuaXR5LmlvL2ltYWdlcy9mdXZiampscC9wcm9kdWN0aW9uLzM0MjNhMWEzMzg4OGRkNzgwMTgwMWU3NzVhMjY3OTgxOGIxNzA1MmMtMjQwMHgxMjYwLnBuZw.avif)

A foundation for AI-assisted development
----------------------------------------

These pieces (a scriptable CLI, a programmable Editor, and a live REPL) add up to more than convenience. They’re what make the demo at the top of this post possible, and they turn Unity into an environment an AI agent can actually work in.

AI coding assistants are good at writing code and content. They've historically struggled with everything around that: running the project, seeing what broke, trying again. An assistant can generate a gameplay script but can't run the tests to see if it works. The Unity CLI and Pipeline layer close that gap.

Two properties make the difference. First, the CLI speaks a language agents understand: structured JSON and a predictable exit-code contract mean a model gets clean, parseable results instead of scraped console text. The same qualities that make it reliable in CI make it reliable as a tool an agent calls.

Second, the Pipeline package makes the Editor self-describing: run _unity command_ with no arguments and a connected Editor reports the operations it exposes. An agent discovers what it can do at runtime instead of relying on a hardcoded list. And because commands are registered with simple attributes, your team can expose project-specific operations as agent-callable tools. This means that each registered command maps naturally into the kind of tool an agent already knows how to invoke.

Put those together and you get a real feedback loop: an assistant can open the project, apply a change, run the tests, enter Play mode to check behavior, read the result, and decide what to do next, with no human relaying output back and forth. That's the shift from an assistant that _suggests_ to one that can _verify_. It's also a natural fit for emerging agent standards: each registered command maps onto the kind of tool a function-calling model or MCP server already knows how to invoke.

And there's no fixed list of what an agent can do. Because _eval_ reaches whatever API your project can call, an agent's capability surface is the same as Unity's: rendering, physics, animation, the asset database, the Editor itself, plus everything your own code adds. That reach is the result of more than a decade of API work, and an agent gets it without any extra integration.

![One pipe to Unity's entire API](https://mip.web.unity.com/img/hyrKw3P5LroC2l3U3eWRgvmaHXwVi5jLg4GW5O5J0io/w:3588/h:1920/q:75/f:avif/aHR0cHM6Ly9jZG4uc2FuaXR5LmlvL2ltYWdlcy9mdXZiampscC9wcm9kdWN0aW9uLzVmM2MyY2Y1YmRhNzI2ZjJmNTBlOWU4YzgzOTJiMTM1N2ZiYTRkYmUtMzU4OHgxOTIwLnBuZw.avif)

One pipe to Unity's entire API

We're at the beginning of this, and the primitives are already here today. If you're building AI-assisted tooling for Unity, the Pipeline package is where to start.

How it relates to Unity’s AI offerings
--------------------------------------

If you use Unity’s AI offerings, such as the in-Editor assistant suite, this is the layer underneath it. Unity’s AI is the part that reasons about your project and decides what to do. The CLI and the Pipeline package are the execution surface that carries those decisions out: fast, local, and token-gated. The same surface is open to any agent, whether that's Unity's own tooling routing through its MCP server, a third-party assistant, or a script you write yourself. Unity’s AI is one consumer of it, not a replacement for it.

Available now
-------------

The Unity CLI is here. Install it, run _unity --help_, and fold it into your next build script or CI job, or automate it with an agent. The [documentation](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli) has the full command reference. Tell us what you build; your feedback shapes where it goes next.

1.  [Unity CLI](/en-us/unity-cli)

Use the Unity command-line interface (CLI)
==========================================

Install the Unity CLI standalone binary and use it to install Editors, add modules, and open projects from a terminal.

Read time 13 minutes

Last updated 11 days ago

* * *

Note

If you use Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Google Antigravity, install the [Unity plugin](/en-us/ai/unity-plugin/about-unity-plugin) for your agent. The plugin includes the

    unity-cli

skill and other Unity skills. Otherwise, install the skills directly from the [Unity Skills repository](https://github.com/Unity-Technologies/skills/blob/main/README.md).

Use the Unity CLI to install Unity Editors, add modules, and manage projects from a terminal. The CLI is a standalone binary that works in CI pipelines, automation scripts, and terminal-first workflows.

The Unity CLI works well for:

*   Continuous integration (CI) pipelines and build agents.
*   Scripting and automation that needs structured output (JSON or TSV) and predictable exit codes.
*   Users who prefer a terminal-first workflow for installing Editors, managing modules, and opening projects.

For command syntax, options, and flags, refer to [Unity CLI reference](/en-us/unity-cli/reference). If you have existing scripts that use the Hub CLI's

    -- --headless

syntax, refer to [Migrate from the Hub CLI](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/migrate-hub-cli) for a comparison of syntax and behavior changes.

Note

To use the Unity CLI to control the Unity Editor, install and set up the [Unity Pipeline package](/en-us/unity-cli/unity-pipeline/unity-pipeline-package). For an example of how you can use the Unity CLI with Unity Pipeline, refer to the [Unity CLI introduction video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DgNrgZeJOxQ).

[](#compatibility)Compatibility
-------------------------------

The Unity CLI is compatible with the following operating systems:

*   Windows 10 21H1 or newer.
*   Linux RHEL 9 and Ubuntu 22.04 and later. Requires glibc 2.34 or newer. Debian 11, CentOS 8, Amazon Linux 2 aren't supported.
*   macOS 14 and newer.

Note

You can install the Unity CLI on headless machines, such as CI workers and build agents. The CLI is also distributed as a Homebrew cask,

    .deb

and

    .rpm

packages, an AppImage, and an MSIX package on Windows. To learn more, refer to [install with a package manager](#install-with-a-package-manager).

[](#common-unity-cli-tasks)Common Unity CLI tasks
-------------------------------------------------

The following commands cover the most common CLI tasks:

unity --help                                # Top-level helpunity install lts                           # Install the latest LTS Editorunity install-modules -e 6000.3.7f1 -m ios  # Add the iOS moduleunity editors -i                            # List installed Editorsunity open ./MyProject                      # Open a projectunity shell                                 # Run many commands in one interactive sessionunity doctor                                # Print a diagnostic snapshot

[](#install-the-unity-cli)Install the Unity CLI
-----------------------------------------------

To install the Unity CLI:

1.  Open a terminal. On Windows, use PowerShell.
2.  Run the install script for your operating system.

macOS or LinuxWindows (PowerShell)

curl -fsSL https://unity.com/install.sh | bash

After the script completes, verify the CLI is available by running

    unity --version

. If the command isn't found, add the install directory to your shell's

    PATH

or reopen your terminal.

On Linux, the script installs the binary to

    ~/.local/bin/unity

, which is on

    PATH

by default on most distributions. Re-running the installer migrates an install from the previous

    ~/.unity

location.

Note

On Linux, the install script and the

    .deb

and

    .rpm

packages check for glibc 2.34 or newer before installation. This means that an unsupported system uses the CLI it already has and doesn't replace it with one that can't start.

The install script above is the recommended way to install the Unity CLI. It always installs the latest release, and

    unity self-update

keeps the CLI current after installation (refer to [Update the Unity CLI](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/cli-config-diagnostics-commands#update-the-unity-cli)). If you already manage command-line tools with a package manager, you can use one of the alternatives below:

To install to a different directory, set

    UNITY_CLI_HOME

before you run the script. The script then installs the CLI to

    <UNITY_CLI_HOME>/bin

(

    <UNITY_CLI_HOME>\bin

on Windows) instead of the default location.

*   Homebrew: update through that package manager instead of
    
        unity self-update
    
*   Linux package repositories: update through that package manager instead of
    
        unity self-update
    
*   winget: winget is the exception, it installs an MSIX package, so
    
        unity self-update
    
    keeps working

### [](#install-with-a-package-manager)Install with a package manager

Homebrew (macOS, Linux)winget (Windows)Linux package repositories (apt, dnf)

On macOS and Linux, you can install the CLI with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh) instead of the install script, so Homebrew keeps it current:

Important

If you installed the Unity CLI from the install script and then install the Homebrew cask, the CLI warns you.

    which unity

continues to resolves to the self-installed copy, and

    brew upgrade

updates the other. The two installations can then drift apart. Run

    unity self-uninstall -y

to remove the self-installed copy and let Homebrew manage updates.

brew install --cask unity-cli

The cask supports Apple silicon and Intel on macOS, and x64 and arm64 on Linux. On Linux, installing casks requires Homebrew 6.0 or later.

To update the CLI, run

    brew upgrade unity-cli

.

Note

The cask installs the command as

    unity

. The cask name is

    unity-cli

because

    unity

refers to a different package in some package managers.

On Windows, you can install the CLI with [winget](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/package-manager/) instead of the install script:

winget install Unity.CLI

To update the CLI, run

    winget upgrade Unity.CLI

.

Note

winget shows the four-part package version, such as

    1.0.0.20005

, because package versions can't include a prerelease tag.

    unity --version

reports the full version, such as

    1.0.0-beta.5

.

On Linux, you can install the CLI from Unity's apt and rpm repositories instead of using the install script. Your system package manager then keeps the CLI current. Beta releases are published to the

    unstable

suite; general availability (GA) releases publish to

    stable

.

To register the repository and install the CLI on Debian or Ubuntu:

curl -sL https://hub.unity3d.com/linux/keys/public | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/Unity\_Technologies\_ApS.gpgsudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/unity-cli.sources <<'EOF'Types: debURIs: https://hub.unity3d.com/linux/repos/debSuites: unstableComponents: mainSigned-By: /usr/share/keyrings/Unity\_Technologies\_ApS.gpgEOFsudo apt update && sudo apt install unity-cli

To register the repository and install the CLI on Fedora or RHEL:

sudo tee /etc/yum.repos.d/unity-cli.repo <<'EOF'\[unity-cli\]name=Unity CLIbaseurl=https://hub.unity3d.com/linux/repos/rpm/unstableenabled=1gpgcheck=1gpgkey=https://hub.unity3d.com/linux/repos/rpm/unstable/repodata/repomd.xml.keyrepo\_gpgcheck=1EOFsudo dnf install unity-cli

If you install a release's

    .deb

or

    .rpm

package file directly, the package registers the matching repository during installation, so

    apt upgrade

or

    dnf upgrade

keeps the CLI current from then on.

Note

The package installs the command as

    unity

. The package name is

    unity-cli

because

    unity

refers to a different package on some distributions.

[](#update-the-unity-cli)Update the Unity CLI
---------------------------------------------

To update the CLI to the latest release:

1.  Open a terminal.
2.  Run the self-update command:

unity self-update

The CLI replaces the current binary with the latest available release. If a download is interrupted, the next

    unity self-update

resumes the download instead of starting over. The CLI also checks for updates in the background and prints a notice when a new release is available. To turn the check off, run

    unity config update-check off

.

    unity upgrade

still works as an alias for

    unity self-update

.

If you installed the CLI with Homebrew or from the Linux package repositories, update it through that package manager instead.

    unity self-update

detects the package-managed install and shows the matching command. A winget install is the exception, since it's an MSIX package,

    unity self-update

continues to update it directly.

### [](#install-a-specific-unity-cli-version)Install a specific Unity CLI version

To install a specific version of the Unity CLI instead of the latest release, run the following self-update command in a terminal with the

    --target

option and the version to install:

unity self-update --target <version>

    unity upgrade

is an alias for

    unity self-update

, so the following command has the same result:

unity upgrade --target <version>

Replace

    <version>

with a release version such as

    1.0.0

. The

    --target

option also accepts a leading

    v

, such as

    v1.0.0

, and

    latest

for the latest release.

Tip

To review the release notes for the version before you install it, run

    unity changelog --target <version>

.

If you installed the CLI with Homebrew or from the Linux package repositories, use that package manager to install a specific version.

### [](#limits-on-automatic-updates)Limits on automatic updates

The following limits apply to automatic updates of the Unity CLI:

*   The Unity Hub updates the Unity CLI automatically. You can't disable these updates in the Hub.
*       unity config update-check off
    
    disables only the CLI's notice that a new release is available. It doesn't stop the Hub from updating the CLI.
*   If you installed the CLI as an MSIX package, including through winget, Windows keeps the CLI current in the background. Rollback isn't available for MSIX installs.
*   If you installed the CLI with Homebrew or from the Linux package repositories, the package manager controls updates.
    
        unity self-update
    
    doesn't update these installs.

### [](#update-with-a-package-manager)Update with a package manager

Homebrew (macOS, Linux)winget (Windows)Linux package repositories (apt, dnf)

brew upgrade unity-cli

winget upgrade Unity.CLI

Note

If you installed the CLI as an MSIX package, including through winget,

    unity self-update

also updates it directly. It downloads only the parts of the package that changed and registers the install with Windows, so it stays current in the background. Rollback isn't available for MSIX installs.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade unity-cli   # Debian and Ubuntu

sudo dnf upgrade unity-cli                      # Fedora and RHEL

To see what the CLI resolved and which command updates your install, run:

unity diagnose update

[](#install-a-unity-editor)Install a Unity Editor
-------------------------------------------------

To install a Unity Editor:

1.  Open a terminal.
2.  Run
    
        unity install
    
    with the version you want. Use a version alias such as
    
        lts
    
    or a specific version string such as
    
        6000.3.7f1
    
    :

unity install ltsunity install 6000.3.7f1

The Editor downloads and installs to the configured install path.

To add modules at install time, use

    -m

followed by one or more module IDs:

unity install lts -m ios android webgl

For all options, version aliases, and module IDs, refer to [Unity CLI reference](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/editor-project-commands#install-an-editor).

[](#add-modules-to-an-installed-editor)Add modules to an installed Editor
-------------------------------------------------------------------------

Important

You can only add modules to Editors installed through the Hub or the CLI. Reinstall manually installed Editors through the Hub or CLI before adding modules.

To add modules to an Editor you already installed:

1.  Open a terminal.
2.  Run
    
        unity install-modules
    
    with
    
        -e
    
    for the Editor version and
    
        -m
    
    for the module IDs:

unity install-modules -e 6000.3.7f1 -m android ios

The modules download and install for the specified Editor version.

For all options and module IDs, refer to [Unity CLI reference](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/editor-project-commands#install-modules-for-an-existing-editor).

[](#create-a-project)Create a project
-------------------------------------

To create a new Unity project:

1.  Open a terminal.
2.  Run
    
        unity projects create
    
    with a project name:

unity projects create MyGame

By default,

    unity projects create

enables Unity Cloud for the new project and creates a Unity Cloud project entry in your organization. The command doesn't upload files, assets, or settings, and it doesn't store or host the local project anywhere. Because the default creates a cloud project, the command needs a signed-in user account. If you aren't signed in, the command stops with exit code 3 before creating anything and names both

    unity auth login

and

    --no-cloud

. The same applies when you authenticate as a service account because service accounts can't create projects in an organization.

To create a local-only project, pass

    --no-cloud

unity projects create MyGame --no-cloud

To keep an entire pipeline local, set

    UNITY_NO_CLOUD

for the job.

To use an existing Unity Cloud project instead of creating one, pass

    --cloud-project <id-or-name>

. You can't combine

    --no-cloud

with

    --cloud

,

    --cloud-org

, or

    --cloud-project

. If the cloud setup doesn't complete, you keep the local project and the command reports a warning.

For all options, run

    unity projects create --help

. For the other

    projects

subcommands, refer to [Unity CLI reference](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/editor-project-commands#manage-projects-in-the-hub-registry).

[](#open-a-project)Open a project
---------------------------------

To open a Unity project:

1.  Open a terminal.
2.  Run
    
        unity open
    
    with the path to the project:

unity open ./MyProject

Unity opens the project in the Editor version specified in the project's settings.

You can omit the

    open

keyword when the first argument is a path:

unity ./MyProject

[](#set-up-version-control)Set up version control
-------------------------------------------------

To add a Unity project to version control:

1.  Open a terminal in the project's directory.
2.  Run:

unity vcs setup

    unity vcs setup

guides you through creating a repository and pushing the first commit. It detects available information, such as whether the project is already in a repository and which Git providers you have signed in to on the machine. It asks only for information it can't detect. Each guided run prints the flags that reproduce the selected configuration. Use

    --save-preset <name>

to save those choices as the default for later runs. The command accepts the same

    --git-*

flags as

    unity projects link vcs

, so so you can skip the questions in scripted runs:

unity vcs setup --vcs github --git-namespace my-org --non-interactive

For the full command tree, including status and sync, repository audits, hooks, conflict resolution, and diffs, refer to [Unity CLI reference](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/uvcs-commands).

[](#sign-in)Sign in
-------------------

To sign in to your Unity account:

1.  Open a terminal.
2.  Run the login command, which opens a browser-based sign-in flow:

unity auth login

The CLI stores your session so you can use other commands without signing in again.

To check whether you're signed in, run

    unity auth status

. For all auth commands, refer to [Unity CLI reference](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/accounts-licenses-cloud-commands#sign-in-and-out).

### [](#sign-in-as-a-service-account)Sign in as a service account

For unattended workflows such as CI pipelines and build agents, you can authenticate with a service account. This is the same service account type used to sign into other Unity services, it isn't specific to the CLI. To learn how to create a service account, refer to [Service accounts](/en-us/cloud/accounts/create-service-account).

To sign in automatically through the Unity CLI, set the

    UNITY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID

and

    UNITY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_SECRET

environment variables to the account's key ID and secret key. For the full list of environment variables, refer to [Unity CLI reference](/en-us/unity-cli/reference/output-formats#environment-variables).

[](#view-long-command-output)View long command output
-----------------------------------------------------

Commands with long listings, such as

    unity releases

,

    unity editors

,

    unity changelog

,

    unity logs

, and the bare

    unity command

listing, page human-readable output through a terminal pager when you run them in an interactive terminal. This prevents long lists from flooding your scrollback, similar to

    git log

. Only human-readable output uses the pager: machine formats such as,

    --format json

, piped or redirected output,

    --quiet

, and commands run inside

    unity shell

print directly:

unity releases

Set

    UNITY_PAGER

or

    PAGER

to use a different pager. Pass

    --no-pager

to turn off paging for a single run, or set

    UNITY_NO_PAGER

to turn off paging for all runs. If no pager is available, output prints directly instead of failing. his is common on Windows, where less isn't installed by default.

Use the Unity Pipeline package to control the Unity Editor remotely through a local HTTP API. Use it to integrate the Unity Editor with CI/CD pipelines, automate testing and development workflows, and execute custom commands from the Unity CLI.

[](#prerequisites)Prerequisites
-------------------------------

Before you start, make sure you meet the following prerequisite:

*   Install the [Unity Editor](/en-us/hub/add-editor) version 6.0 or later
*   Install the [Unity CLI](/en-us/unity-cli/use-unity-cli)

[](#install-unity-pipeline-package)Install Unity Pipeline package
-----------------------------------------------------------------

To install the Unity Pipeline package:

1.  Close and reopen your terminal after you install the Unity CLI.
2.  Open your project in the Unity Editor.
3.  Open a Terminal window (macOS) or Powershell (Windows).
4.  Run
    
        unity auth login
    
    to sign in.
5.  Run
    
        unity pipeline install
    
    to install the Unity Pipeline package and its dependencies. By default, the command targets the current directory or the running Editor instance.
6.  Return to the Unity Editor and wait for the project to recompile with the new Unity Pipeline package
7.  In the terminal, run
    
        unity pipeline editors
    
    to verify the installation.

Verify that **Pipeline: Installed** appears, as shown in the following screenshot.

Unity Pipeline package is successfully installed

[](#connect-to-a-running-unity-editor)Connect to a running Unity Editor

After you install the Unity Pipeline package, connect to a running Unity Editor to view the available commands.

*   To automatically discover a Unity project from the current directory, run
    
        unity command
    
    .
*   If you have more than one Unity Editor instance open, run
    
        unity command --project-path=<path-to-your-project>
    
    to connect to a specific Unity project.

Sources: P1 = https://unity.com/the-unity-cli-1.0-is-here (Nov 17, 2026 post), P2 = https://unity.com/blog/meet-the-unity-cli (Jul 20, 2026 post), P3 = https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/release-notes/2026/november (release notes; the tail of this page was a model summary, so facts from that part are marked). I also read two pages linked from these: D1 = https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/use-unity-cli and D2 = https://docs.unity.com/en-us/unity-cli/unity-pipeline/unity-pipeline-package.

**a) Linux install and supported systems**
- Install script (D1): `curl -fsSL https://unity.com/install.sh | bash`. On Linux it installs to `~/.local/bin/unity`. D1 calls this "the recommended way."
- Install script in P2 (July, older): `curl -fsSL https://public-cdn.cloud.unity3d.com/hub/prod/cli/install.sh | UNITY_CLI_CHANNEL=beta bash`. P2 also said apt/brew/winget support was "coming soon." P1 says the CLI is available "through Homebrew, winget and APT."
- APT (D1), Debian/Ubuntu:
  - Key: `curl -sL https://hub.unity3d.com/linux/keys/public | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/Unity_Technologies_ApS.gpg`
  - Source file `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/unity-cli.sources` with `Types: deb`, `URIs: https://hub.unity3d.com/linux/repos/deb`, `Suites: unstable` (beta; GA uses `stable`), `Components: main`, `Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/Unity_Technologies_ApS.gpg`
  - Then `sudo apt update && sudo apt install unity-cli`. The package installs the command as `unity`.
- RPM (D1), Fedora/RHEL: repo at `https://hub.unity3d.com/linux/repos/rpm/unstable` (gpgcheck on), then `sudo dnf install unity-cli`.
- Homebrew (D1): `brew install --cask unity-cli`. Linux casks need Homebrew 6.0 or later. Also available as AppImage and .deb/.rpm files.
- Supported OS (D1, "Compatibility"): Windows 10 21H1 or newer; "Linux RHEL 9 and Ubuntu 22.04 and later. Requires glibc 2.34 or newer. Debian 11, CentOS 8, Amazon Linux 2 aren't supported."; macOS 14 and newer.
- D1 says the CLI "can be installed on headless machines, such as CI workers and build agents."

**b) Authentication and licensing**
- Interactive: `unity auth login` "opens a browser-based sign-in flow" (D1). `unity auth status` checks sign-in.
- Service account for CI (D1): set `UNITY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID` and `UNITY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_SECRET` to the key ID and secret key. P2 says a headless build agent "authenticates with a service account via environment variables."
- Service accounts cannot create cloud projects (D1). `unity projects create` needs a signed-in user unless `--no-cloud` is passed.
- P3 (release notes, summary part): `UNITY_CLOUD_PROJECT` should be set to the project ID the token is for. Also `unity auth login --insecure-storage` exists (P3, verbatim part).
- P1 says the "Build Server license now covers agents and automation... one license per instance lets you run agents on a headless Editor or in a container."
- None of the pages I read mention Unity ID specifically, Personal vs Pro activation, or the exact license-activation steps for a headless Editor. P3 mentions `unity license return` returning "Assigned seats such as Unity Pro." Whether an Editor on a CI machine can be activated under a Personal license is not stated.

**c) Pipeline package (com.unity.pipeline)**
- P2: "lets a running Editor receive commands from the CLI entirely on your machine," and works "with Unity 6.0 LTS and newer." It is "experimental" per P2 (July). P1 says the CLI and Pipeline package "are out of beta."
- D2: "Control the Unity Editor through a local HTTP API to automate builds, tests, and development workflows." Prerequisites: Unity Editor 6.0 or later and the Unity CLI.
- Install (D2): close and reopen the terminal, open the project in the Editor, run `unity auth login`, then `unity pipeline install` ("targets the current directory or the running Editor instance"), wait for recompile, then `unity pipeline editors` to verify "Pipeline: Installed."
- Agent use (P2): `unity command` lists commands; `unity command <name>` runs one. `unity command eval "return Application.version;"` runs C# in the running Editor (Roslyn, main thread), "gated behind a security token." Custom commands use `[CliCommand]` and `[CliArg]`. `--runtime <player exec name>` targets a dev Player build; "localhost-only and off by default."
- `--project-path=<path>` selects one Editor when several are open (D2).
- P1: `unity build --target` "builds in the Editor that has the project open." `unity open --until-ready` waits until the Editor can take commands. `unity projects create` adds the Pipeline package to new projects.
- Batch mode: neither D2 nor P2 describes batch-mode Editor runs. P3 (verbatim part) says `unity assets import` and `unity open --batchmode` now work on Linux with no display.

**d) Headless or container Editor**
- P1: "Coming soon: the Linux containerized Editor, a supported headless Unity Editor in a Linux container, built for CI, build machines and agents." Its status is still "coming soon" as of P1.
- Headless use of the CLI itself is supported (D1, P2). The "Build Server license... on a headless Editor or in a container" wording in P1 is the only mention of container use.
- No page I read says whether the Editor runs without a GPU. The only related statement is the P3 `--batchmode` / no-display item above.

**e) Android modules and Unity 6.3 LTS**
- P2: `unity install 6000.2.10f1 -m android ios webgl` and `unity install 6000.2.10f1 -m android ios --accept-eula --yes`.
- D1: `unity install lts -m ios android webgl`, and `unity install-modules -e 6000.3.7f1 -m android ios`. `-m` takes module IDs.
- D1 example version: `unity install 6000.3.7f1`.
- P3 (summary part): fallback versions "Unity 6000.0.85f2 and 6000.3.28f1 LTS." No page says "6.3 LTS" literally; 6000.3.x is the 6.3 line.
- P3 (summary part): `unity editors module add` and `unity install-modules` exist. Android-specific `--android-*` flags exist, but the summary did not list them.
- No Android module ID list was found.

**f) Claude Code, agent plugins, MCP**
- P1: "official Unity plugins for Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build and Google Antigravity." Skills come from GitHub `Unity-Technologies/skills`.
- P1: `unity setup` "installs the official plugin for Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build or Google Antigravity." `unity skill install --all` and `unity skill sync` cover other agents. `unity setup all` installs skills.
- P3 (summary part): `unity mcp configure <client>` and `unity mcp configure --list` exist. `unity mcp --tools` and `--exclude-tools` filter commands. A docs page titled "Replace MCP Server with Unity CLI" exists (D1 link list) but was not read.
- P2: each registered command "maps onto the kind of tool a function-calling model or MCP server already knows how to invoke."
- P1 says the official plugin "gives the agent skills," including "building UI, setting up lighting or adding in-app purchases."
